title: Outage: a month-end report starves the order API of CPU

objective: Diagnose and manage processes: find them with ps, top and pgrep, change priority, and send the right signal
secondaryObjectives: Monitor and troubleshoot system performance: load, CPU, memory and I/O with uptime, top, free and vmstat
Troubleshoot a service that fails to start using systemctl status, journalctl and its unit file

sources.cite: Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator (LFCS): Domains & Competencies, Operations Deployment 25%
sources.note: Relevant text: Operations Deployment, 'Diagnose, identify, manage, and troubleshoot processes and services'; Operations Deployment, 'Manage and troubleshoot system performance'. Read as the page's HTML on 2026-11-14 (page last modified 2026-10-30).

Relevant text: 'On modern Linux, the range is -20 (high priority) to +19 (low priority)'; under CFS each unit of difference in nice value 'results in a factor of 1.25 in the degree to which the scheduler favors the higher priority process'; 'on Linux, the nice value is a per-thread attribute'. Read through a summarizing fetch 2026-11-14.

Relevant text: 'renice alters the scheduling priority of one or more running processes'; -p 'Interpret the succeeding arguments as process IDs (the default)'; 'an unprivileged user can only increase the "nice value"'; 'The superuser may alter the priority of any process'. Read through a summarizing fetch 2026-11-14.

Relevant text: kill(1), 'If no signal is specified, the TERM signal is sent' and 'If a process does not terminate after a TERM signal has been sent, then the KILL signal may be used'; signal(7), 'The signals SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored'. Both read through summarizing fetches 2026-11-14. That a SIGKILLed PostgreSQL server must run crash recovery on restart is the database's documented behavior after an unclean stop; the minutes it takes here are authored.

brief.situation: You are the on-call administrator for api1, an 8-CPU server that runs the order API and its PostgreSQL database for Larkspur Logistics (fictional). Since about 09:55 the API has been slow, and the latency agreement is breached if it stays over 1 second until 10:32. Finance started the quarter-close report on this host at 09:50; the controller needs it by noon, and it takes about 70 minutes on its own.
handover: The report is /opt/reports/qclose.py, run by the user fin; it uses one worker process per core it finds.
Nothing was deployed to the API this week.
howItWorks: Run commands from the command line: type one, or pick it from the suggestions or the action list. Only this lab's commands run; there is no free shell, and each command's arguments are fixed.
Each command takes operator time: run it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The outage keeps developing on the same clock.
The map shows each host, disk or service and the links between them, with a status in words. Output appears in the terminal as it happens.
When you declare the service restored, you write the incident record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: How many operator minutes each command takes, and when the fictional outage spreads, are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values. The latency agreement is breached at 10:32, 30 minutes after the start.

writeup.question: For the incident record: what slowed the API, how you showed it, and why you chose that fix over the others.

parts.label: Cause
parts.criteria: Names the report's worker processes running at nice 0 on every CPU, with postgres busy as a symptom, not the cause.
parts.modelAnswer: qclose.py started eight workers at nice 0; with load at 16 on 8 CPUs, the API's processes waited for CPU and its queries piled up in postgres.

parts.label: Evidence
parts.criteria: Uses uptime or top and pgrep (or ps) to find the processes and their nice values before changing anything.
parts.modelAnswer: top showed eight python3 processes owned by fin at about 97% each and NI 0; pgrep -a -u fin listed the parent and its workers.

parts.label: Fix and trade-off
parts.criteria: Renices the parent and every worker to 19 rather than killing the report (finance needs it by noon) or touching postgres; explains that renicing only the parent changes nothing for the workers; checks the API.
parts.modelAnswer: renice -n 19 -p $(pgrep -u fin -f qclose) put all nine processes at 19, about 1.25^19 (roughly 70 times) less favored than the API at 0, so the API is fast again and the report still finishes on spare CPU; curl showed 0.18 s.

expertPath.text: uptime (load 16 on 8 CPUs) and top: eight python3 processes owned by fin at NI 0; postgres is busy because the API is waiting.
pgrep -a -u fin python3: the quarter-close parent and its eight workers. Finance needs this report by noon, so do not stop it.
renice -n 19 -p $(pgrep -u fin -f qclose): all nine, not just the parent.
curl the health endpoint (0.18 s); record it, and suggest finance runs it under nice or on the reporting host.

fixed.headline: Good: both kept
fixed.body: You found the workers, lowered all of them, and the API got its CPU back while the report kept going.

fixedGaps.headline: Fast again, with gaps
fixedGaps.body: The result is right. The criteria show what it cost: time, or a change made before you looked.

reportLost.headline: API back, report lost
reportLost.body: Stopping the report fixed the API but cost finance its noon deadline. A nice value of 19 against 0 gives the API about 70 times the report's share of CPU.

dbKilled.headline: Database killed
dbKilled.body: postgres was busy because the API was waiting, not the cause. SIGKILL gives it no chance to shut down cleanly.

stillSlow.headline: Closed too soon
stillSlow.body: Renicing the parent alone does not change its workers: each process has its own nice value. Check NI in ps or top for every worker.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Load 16 on 8 CPUs with eight python3 workers at NI 0: the report is taking the CPUs. Finance needs it, so lower its priority instead of stopping it: renice every process (pgrep gives all the PIDs), since renicing the parent leaves the running workers at 0. Under CFS each nice step is a factor of 1.25, so 19 against 0 lets the API run first. Never kill postgres, which is only a symptom.
